title: Restore the decision in qm75 (three-way duel)
summary: qm75 removed the choice that makes this puzzle famous: the weakest shooter's best move is to miss on purpose. Restoring the choice needs an assumption about how the other two aim, so it is proposed here rather than published.

decision.subject: qm75 · three-way duel
decision.context: Restoring A's choice needs one assumption: B and C aim at the more accurate remaining shooter. With it, deliberately missing is best (0.300).

options.label: Rewrite with this assumption
options.effect: Replace qm75 with the decision version (answer becomes 0.300)

options.label: Other
options.effect: Tell me what you want instead

question.title: Three Shooters, One Choice
question.description: Three shooters, A, B and C, take turns in the order A → B → C, skipping anyone who has been hit, until one remains. A hits with probability 0.3, B always hits, and C hits with probability 0.5. B and C always aim at the more accurate of their remaining opponents. On A's first turn only, A may shoot at B, shoot at C, or deliberately miss; after that A also aims at the more accurate opponent. If A makes the best first choice, what is A's probability of being the last one standing? Enter a decimal to 3 decimal places.

steps.label: Deliberately miss
steps.value: B removes C; A then shoots first at B and wins with 0.3

question.explanation: Hitting someone hurts A: whoever survives then shoots at A with only two left. Missing on purpose lets B and C fight first and gives A the first shot of a two-way duel. A's chance in a duel against C when C shoots first is 0.5 × 0.3 / 0.65 ≈ 0.231.

reasoningPattern: Strategic decision with recursion on states: compare the value of each first move.

sources.note: The existing qm75 appears to derive from the version in Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability (1965); this is an audit observation, not checked against the book

authenticity.rationale: Asks for a decision against opponents and rewards a counter-intuitive insight, which is what interviewers probe. Widely published, so some candidates will know the answer.

verification: Exact values 0.3, 0.2792 and 0.21 derived by hand; a Monte Carlo run of 1,000,000 duels per choice gave 0.2994, 0.2792 and 0.2104.
openQuestions: Assumption: B and C aim at the more accurate remaining opponent. This is the classic convention, but it is an assumption; approve it or suggest another.
The answer changes from 0.2308 (the old question asked something narrower) to 0.300.
